Yeah, good question. In "Isaac", the profanity, horribleness and bad taste all serve the purpose of going over the top and making you augh about it. It's crazy, but it's entertaining, and I even think it's healthy to some degree that one gets to "experience" these issues (oh let's see, birth defects, abortion, child abuse/beating, religious/racial slurs... the list goes on) which are otherwise completely taboo, in a game. And after all, you play as Isaac who is the recipient of all this evil, but you are fighting against it and get to feel sympathy for him.

Hatred is different, because you are supposed to simply kill innocent people. That's all. I haven't played the game but I don't think there is quality humor there, and neither do I think it serves any purpose as "venting" - who needs to vent about killing innocent people at bus stops? Similar themes - mayhem, destruction I guess, have appeared in other pieces of art (take Fight Club) but there it was always for some "purpose", some greater goal, or there was some undergoing moral story, character development or something like that. In Hatred, there is nothing more - just the killing.

All in all, I'd say violence and brutality can serve multiple purposes in a game, but in Hatred, it serves none. And that's why I don't like it.

Based on what little bit of Hatred I played: meh.

The uncensored ugliness of Isaac works well partially because it leaves you wondering what you'll find next, and makes you feel bad for the protagonist. It largely resembles the worst nightmares of a child, hence the mix of the cartoon style and the morbid topics, and is the best possible fit for the topic at hand.

In Hatred, there is messed up stuff, but it doesn't seem to develop over time or relate to anyone's struggles. It doesn't lead to better enemy or level design. It just feels coated on.

You know that TF2 short "Meet the Pyro?" Hatred feels kind of like that, just in another direction.

Note that I have only played a bit of Hatred (the $20 price discouraged me), so I could be wrong.
